messages.author: 5abdb409f213d464
messages.subject: Re: invariance output interpretation
parts:
It is difficult to answer when invariance can be defended and which test should be performed (is the chisquare test significant for fit.configural?). I personally would think that there is enough evidence that nothing is invariant after fit.loadings.
With parTable() you can determine what .p20. etc. refers to. Hope that helps.

messages.author: 9b7a59c6f2d552cc
messages.subject: Re: invariance output interpretation
parts:
you can tell that you have metric equivalence because the change in chisq relative to the change in df has a p >.05. This tells you that fixing the metric loadings of factors to items to be equal between groups causes very little change in the fit of the model to the data. The test for equivalent intercepts shows that the fit changes by much more than would be expected by chance. Even the change in CFI is much larger than the recommended .01 for this equivalence. So you have equivalent loadings but not intercepts. In a repeated measures study where the 2 groups are the same people at 2 times, this would be enough to allow comparison of group means. However, in a cross-sectional study, these 2 groups differ at their intercept or starting points by more than chance. Investigating which items have different intercepts becomes the question of interest. Are you able to speculate as to the cause of the difference--in what way are the 2 groups different? This suggests your groups do NOT come from the same population.
you can read a helpful tutorial on this matter in:
Brown, G. T. L., Harris, L. R., O'Quin, C., & Lane, K. E. (2017). Using multi-group confirmatory factor analysis to evaluate cross-cultural research: Identifying and understanding non-invariance. International Journal of Research & Method in Education, 40(1), 66-90. doi:doi:10.1080/1743727X.2015.1070823
